gentle.ch01-the-truth-about-relativity: Ariely opens with a strange magazine offer: The Economist gives readers three subscription choices, and one of them exists mostly to make another option look better. That small setup reveals the chapter's main claim. People rarely judge value on its own. We compare things that sit close together and then let the easier comparison steer us. That is why decoys work. A weak option can push us toward a more expensive one without improving what we truly need. The same habit shows up outside shopping too, when another person's salary, vacation, or home quietly becomes our standard. Relativity helps because life would be slow if we had to measure everything from scratch, but it also makes us vulnerable to manipulation and envy. The practical lesson is to notice when an easy comparison is replacing a better question about actual worth.
gentle.ch02-the-fallacy-of-supply-and-demand: Ariely argues that many prices do not come from a stable inner sense of worth. They often start with an anchor. Once that first number lands, later prices can feel logical even if the starting point was arbitrary. He uses Tahitian black pearls to show this. They did not become luxury items because buyers naturally knew their value. They became luxury items after marketers placed them beside rare gems and priced them high. Ariely then connects this to experiments where random numbers changed what people were willing to pay. The lesson is not that every price is fake. It is that first prices shape later judgment more than people admit. That is why demand is not always a clean reflection of what people independently want. A practical response is to notice the first number that framed your decision and ask whether it deserves that authority.
gentle.ch03-the-cost-of-zero-cost: The Cost of Zero Cost shows that free is psychologically different from merely cheap. Ariely uses the truffle-versus-Kiss candy experiment and the pull of free shipping, trials, and bonus offers. The warning is that zero removes the felt downside and makes people ignore total value, future cost, and clutter. The practical move is to run the one-cent test and recalculate the full outcome before accepting the free option. the chapter does not say every free offer is bad, only that free deserves more comparison, not less.
